sections.title: The biggest crowd on Earth
sections.intro_md:
Between **13 January and 26 February 2025**, a temporary city rose on the sandbanks where the Ganga meets the Yamuna at **Prayagraj**. It had pontoon bridges, hospitals, police stations and its own district administration. The Uttar Pradesh government says about **660 million** people came to bathe in those 45 days. Nobody can count a crowd that size precisely, but even a fraction of that claim would make it the largest gathering of human beings ever recorded.

On **29 January**, the most auspicious bathing day, a crush near the confluence killed at least **30 people** by the official count. Journalists later found more deaths than the state admitted.

That is UP in one scene: faith at a scale nowhere else attempts, a state stretched to its limit, and an argument about numbers. Today: the Buddha's first sermon, the Taj, the nawabs of Lucknow, the birth of Hindi, and the votes that pick India's rulers.

spotlights.name: Maha Kumbh Mela, Prayagraj
spotlights.when: Every 12 years; latest 13 January to 26 February 2025
spotlights.spot_it: Miles of tents on river sand, pontoon bridges, and a solid mass of people wading into brown water at dawn.
spotlights.story_md: The Kumbh rotates between four river cities, but Prayagraj hosts the biggest. A full **Maha Kumbh** comes every 12 years. For 2025 the state built a tent city over about **4,000 hectares** and, in December 2024, declared the mela ground a separate temporary district. The legend: drops of nectar from a pot (*kumbh*) fell at four places. Clear records of the fair date from Mughal and British times. UNESCO listed the Kumbh as intangible heritage in **2017**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest peaceful gathering of people anywhere, and a test of how India runs a city for six weeks.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city the size of a country, built on sand, gone by March.

spotlights.name: Triveni Sangam
spotlights.when: Sacred since at least the Vedic hymns
spotlights.spot_it: Two rivers of different colours meeting: the muddy Ganga and the greener Yamuna, with boats moored at the seam.
spotlights.story_md: *Triveni* means three braids. Two rivers are visible: the Ganga and the Yamuna. The third, the **Saraswati**, is believed to join underground and is invisible by definition, which is why it is a matter of faith rather than geography. Pilgrims hire a boat to the exact meeting point, where wooden platforms let them dip in mid-river. The colour line is real: the Yamuna is usually clearer and darker, the Ganga lighter and silt-heavy. The Mughal emperor **Akbar** built a fort right on the confluence in **1583** and renamed the town Ilahabad. It became Allahabad, and in **2018** the state renamed it Prayagraj.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the holiest river junction in Hinduism and the reason the Kumbh is held here.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two rivers you can see, one you have to believe in.

sections.title: The state at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Uttar Pradesh means 'northern province'. It covers **240,928 km²**, the fourth largest state, and had **199.8 million** people in 2011, more than any other state and more than all but five countries. Official projections put it at roughly **240 million** now. If it were a country, it would sit near Pakistan as the fifth most populous on Earth.

It has **75 districts**, a **403-seat** assembly and sends **80** members to the Lok Sabha, the largest bloc of any state, which is why national politicians say the road to Delhi runs through Lucknow.

The economy is big and spread thin. UP's own first Economic Survey, presented in **February 2026**, puts its 2024-25 output at **₹30.25 lakh crore**, about **9.1%** of India's, among the top three or four states. But income per person, about **₹1.1 lakh**, is only around half the national average. Literacy was **67.7%** in 2011, against 74% nationally.

spotlights.name: Lucknow
spotlights.when: Capital of Awadh from 1775; of the state from the 1920s
spotlights.spot_it: Domed gateways and imambaras in old Lucknow, wide avenues and a glass-and-sandstone skyline in the new.
spotlights.story_md: Lucknow became a royal capital in **1775**, when the Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula moved his court here from Faizabad. For the next 80 years it was the richest court in north India, famous for poetry, kebabs, Kathak and an elaborate politeness. The British annexed it in **1856**, and a year later it was the scene of the longest siege of 1857. Allahabad was the first capital of the United Provinces; government moved to Lucknow in stages during the **1920s**. Today it has about **3.5 million** people and a slogan at the station: *Muskuraiye, aap Lucknow mein hain*, 'Smile, you are in Lucknow'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the seat of power for one in six Indians, and the guardian of a court culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: A nawab moved here in 1775, and the city has been showing off its manners ever since.

sections.title: A plain built by rivers
sections.intro_md:
Most of Uttar Pradesh is one of the flattest, most fertile and most crowded places on Earth: the **Ganga plain**, layers of silt hundreds of metres deep, laid down by rivers coming off the Himalaya. The land drops only a few hundred metres across the whole state. The **Ganga** enters at Bijnor and leaves near Ballia; the **Yamuna** runs parallel past Mathura and Agra and joins it at Prayagraj. The Gomti, Ghaghra, Sharda and Rapti drain the north.

Along the Nepal border lies the **Terai**, a belt of tall grass and sal forest that once covered the whole north and now survives in reserves such as Dudhwa. South of the Yamuna the plain gives way to the rocky, drought-prone plateau of **Bundelkhand** and the Vindhya hills.

Summers pass 45°C; winter fog stops trains.

spotlights.name: The Ganga at Varanasi
spotlights.when: The river; the ghats mostly 18th century
spotlights.spot_it: A wide crescent of river with stone steps, temples and palaces stacked on one bank and empty sand on the other.
spotlights.story_md: At Varanasi the Ganga does something unusual: it bends to flow **north**, toward the Himalaya it came from. Hindus read this as especially sacred. The west bank is lined with more than **80 ghats**, the stone stairways where people bathe, wash, pray, swim and cremate their dead. The east bank is left almost bare, partly by belief and partly because the river floods it every monsoon. Long stretches of the Ganga in UP fail bathing-water standards for faecal bacteria, despite decades of clean-up plans; the river that washes away sins is itself badly in need of washing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the spine of the state's geography and its faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: At Varanasi the holy river turns and walks back toward its source.

spotlights.name: Dudhwa and Billy Arjan Singh
spotlights.spot_it: Terai grassland taller than a person, sal forest edges, and swamps where swamp deer and rhinos feed.
spotlights.story_md: Dudhwa exists largely because of one stubborn man. **Billy Arjan Singh**, a farmer turned conservationist, lobbied for years to protect this corner of the Terai, and it became a national park in **1977**. At his farm, Tiger Haven, he raised a tigress named **Tara**, brought as a cub from a zoo in England, and released her into the forest in **1978**. Critics later argued she carried Siberian tiger genes into the wild population; the claim is still debated. In **1984** Dudhwa received rhinos from Assam and Nepal, returning the species to UP after more than a century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is UP's best surviving piece of the wild Terai, and a test case for rewilding.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tigress from England, rhinos from Assam: Dudhwa was restocked by hand.

spotlights.name: Barasingha, the swamp deer
spotlights.spot_it: A large golden-brown deer standing knee-deep in marsh, the stag with wide antlers carrying many points.
spotlights.story_md: *Barasingha* means 'twelve-tined', and a big stag can indeed carry 10 to 14 points on its antlers. It is the **state animal** of Uttar Pradesh. It is a specialist of wet grassland, and as the Terai was drained for farming in the 20th century its numbers crashed. The northern swamp deer now survive in a few pockets, with **Dudhwa** and the Kishanpur sanctuary among the most important. Unlike most deer it gathers in herds out in open swamp, which once made it easy to shoot.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its survival is a measure of whether any wetland of the old Terai is left.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve tines and wet feet: the deer that needs a swamp to live.

spotlights.name: Gharial of the Chambal
spotlights.spot_it: A long, very thin-snouted crocodile basking on a sandbank, the male with a bulbous knob on the tip of its nose.
spotlights.story_md: The gharial eats fish and almost nothing else, and its pencil-thin snout is built for snapping sideways in water. By the mid-1970s fewer than **200** were left in the wild. The **National Chambal Sanctuary**, set up in **1979** across UP, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, now holds most of the world's wild gharials. The Chambal survives as one of north India's cleanest rivers partly because of a curse: in the Mahabharata it is said to be born of blood, so few towns were built on its banks, and its ravines were for long the country of bandits.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the last stronghold of one of the world's most endangered crocodiles.
spotlights.memory_hook: A snout like a chopstick and a river nobody wanted to live beside.

spotlights.name: Sarus crane
spotlights.spot_it: A grey bird as tall as a person, with a bare red head and neck, usually in a pair in a paddy field.
spotlights.story_md: The sarus is the **tallest flying bird in the world**, standing up to about **1.8 metres**. It is UP's state bird, and the state holds a large share of India's sarus population, mostly living alongside farmers in rice fields and village ponds rather than in reserves. Pairs stay together for years and perform loud duets, heads thrown back. Folk belief holds that a sarus whose mate dies will pine to death, which has protected it from hunting for centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that wildlife in UP survives among people, not apart from them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Taller than you, married for life, and it lives in a rice field.

sections.title: Where the Buddha taught and India got its emblem
sections.intro_md:
Much of what India calls its classical past happened on this plain. The kingdoms of **Kosala** (around Ayodhya and Sravasti) and **Kashi** (Varanasi) were among the great states of the 6th century BCE, when the Buddha walked between their cities. He gave his first sermon at **Sarnath**, spent many rainy seasons at **Sravasti** and died at **Kushinagar**, all in today's UP.

Later, **Mathura** became a great art city under the Kushans in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, making some of the first images of the Buddha in human form. The **Guptas** (4th to 6th centuries) left early stone temples and inscriptions. In the 7th century **Kannauj** was Harsha's capital, and for 200 years three empires fought over it.

Archaeology keeps pushing the story back. At **Sinauli** near Meerut, burials around **4,000 years old** contained copper-sheathed coffins and wheeled vehicles that may be the oldest chariots found in South Asia.

spotlights.name: Dhamek Stupa, Sarnath
spotlights.when: Present form about 500 CE, on older foundations
spotlights.spot_it: A massive, squat brick-and-stone drum about 43 metres high, its lower part carved with flowing floral bands.
spotlights.story_md: Around **528 BCE**, by traditional reckoning, the newly enlightened Buddha walked about 10 km from Varanasi to a deer park and gave his first sermon to five former companions. Buddhists call it the first turning of the wheel of the law. Sarnath grew into a great monastery town under Ashoka and the Guptas. The **Dhamek Stupa**, rebuilt around **500 CE**, is about **43.6 m** high and **28 m** across, and marks the spot by tradition. The site was sacked around the 12th century and forgotten; in **1794** a local official's workers dug bricks from one stupa for a market building and found a relic casket, which started the rediscovery.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Buddhism began as a teaching here, and pilgrims from Sri Lanka to Japan still come.
spotlights.memory_hook: The wheel started turning in a deer park near Varanasi.

spotlights.name: Lion Capital of Ashoka
spotlights.spot_it: Four lions back to back on a drum carved with a wheel, a horse, a bull, an elephant and a lion, all in glassy polished stone.
spotlights.story_md: The capital crowned a pillar Emperor **Ashoka** set up at Sarnath around **250 BCE**. It is carved from one block of **Chunar sandstone**, polished to a mirror sheen that still puzzles people today. A German engineer, **Friedrich Oertel**, dug it up in **1905**. On **26 January 1950** India adopted it as the **State Emblem**, and its 24-spoked wheel went onto the national flag. In the official emblem you can see only three of the four lions; the fourth is hidden behind. The original never leaves the Sarnath Museum.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every Indian passport, coin and court order carries this UP sculpture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four lions, three visible: India's emblem was dug out of a Sarnath field in 1905.

spotlights.name: Mahaparinirvana Temple, Kushinagar
spotlights.spot_it: A white barrel-roofed shrine holding a huge reclining Buddha draped in gold and saffron cloth.
spotlights.story_md: The Buddha died here, lying on his right side between two sal trees, aged about 80. Inside the temple lies a **6.1 m** reclining Buddha carved in the **5th century** from red sandstone brought from Mathura. It had broken and been buried; the British archaeologist **A. C. L. Carlleyle** excavated and restored it in **1876**. Pilgrims cover it in fine cloth, so the stone is rarely seen. Kushinagar got an **international airport in 2021**, aimed at Buddhist pilgrims from Thailand, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Japan.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the four holiest Buddhist sites, and three of the four are in or near UP.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 1,500-year-old Buddha, asleep under a blanket of silk.

spotlights.name: Sinauli chariot burials
spotlights.spot_it: Skeletons laid in wooden coffins whose legs are sheathed in copper, beside the remains of solid-wheeled vehicles.
spotlights.story_md: In **2018** the Archaeological Survey of India dug a field at Sinauli, 70 km from Delhi, and found burials with copper-decorated coffins, swords, a helmet, shields and the remains of **three wheeled vehicles**. Earlier seasons from **2005** had already found more than 100 graves. The dates fall around **2000 to 1800 BCE**. The ASI called the vehicles chariots and the find a warrior elite. Other archaeologists point out that the wheels are solid, not spoked, so they may be carts, and that horses have not been proved. Either way, nothing like it had been found in India before.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It opened an argument about who lived on the Ganga plain 4,000 years ago, and how they fought.
spotlights.memory_hook: Copper-legged coffins and the oldest wheels in the Ganga plain.

spotlights.name: Mathura school: the headless Kanishka
spotlights.spot_it: Speckled red sandstone figures: a full-cheeked, smiling Buddha with a halo, or a stiff royal figure in a long coat and heavy boots.
spotlights.story_md: Mathura's workshops carved in a mottled red sandstone quarried at nearby Sikri. Under the **Kushan** kings they made some of the earliest standing and seated Buddhas in human form, broad-shouldered and smiling, at about the same time as the Greek-influenced school of Gandhara. The most famous Mathura statue is not religious at all: a life-size **headless** figure of King **Kanishka** in a Central Asian riding coat and felt boots, holding a sword and a mace, with his titles inscribed across the hem. The head was never found.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Mathura helped invent the image of the Buddha that Asia still uses.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king with no head, still wearing his riding boots.

sections.title: Marble and red sandstone: the Mughals in Agra
sections.intro_md:
For about a century, from Akbar's reign to Shah Jahan's, **Agra** was one of the capitals of the richest empire in the world. Akbar rebuilt the fort from **1565**, founded a whole new city at **Fatehpur Sikri** in **1571**, and was buried at **Sikandra** outside Agra. His son Jahangir's wife Nur Jahan built a jewel-box tomb for her father. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal and then spent his last eight years locked in the fort looking at it.

The Mughal buildings of UP show a style changing fast: from Akbar's red sandstone, mixing Persian domes with Hindu brackets and Jain-looking pillars, to Shah Jahan's white marble inlaid with semi-precious stones. Three of them, the **Taj Mahal**, **Agra Fort** and **Fatehpur Sikri**, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

spotlights.name: Taj Mahal
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble tomb with a bulb dome, four free-standing minarets and a long water channel in front.
spotlights.story_md: **Mumtaz Mahal** died in **1631** giving birth to her 14th child. Her husband, Shah Jahan, spent about 22 years and the labour of some **20,000** workers building her tomb on the Yamuna. The marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, and the inlay used stones from across Asia. The four minarets lean very slightly **outward**, so that in an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb. The famous story that Shah Jahan cut off the builders' hands has no historical source. Today the marble turns yellow from air pollution and is cleaned with a clay pack called *multani mitti*.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most recognised building in India and a UNESCO site since 1983.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-two years, twenty thousand hands, and none of them cut off.

spotlights.name: Agra Fort
spotlights.spot_it: A long crescent of red sandstone walls on the Yamuna, with white marble pavilions on top.
spotlights.story_md: Akbar rebuilt the fort in red sandstone from **1565**; his grandson Shah Jahan replaced many of the buildings inside with white marble halls. In **1658** Shah Jahan's son **Aurangzeb** seized the throne and kept his father prisoner here. Shah Jahan lived eight more years in the fort and died in **1666** in the **Musamman Burj**, an octagonal marble tower with a view across the river bend to the Taj Mahal. Much of the fort is still used by the Indian Army and closed to visitors.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the seat of Mughal power and the prison of the man who built the Taj.
spotlights.memory_hook: Shah Jahan's last view: his wife's tomb, from his son's jail.

spotlights.name: Tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah, the 'Baby Taj'
spotlights.spot_it: A small, square white marble tomb covered entirely in coloured geometric inlay, with four squat corner towers.
spotlights.story_md: Before the Taj there was this. **Nur Jahan**, the most powerful woman of the Mughal court, built it for her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg, Jahangir's chief minister, titled *Itimad-ud-Daulah*, 'pillar of the state'. It was one of the first Mughal buildings faced in white marble and the first to use **pietra dura** inlay on this scale: wine cups, cypress trees and flower vases set in coloured stone. It is small enough to walk round in five minutes, and much quieter than its famous neighbour.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the design rehearsal for the Taj, commissioned by a woman.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nur Jahan's jewel box: the Taj Mahal's first draft.

spotlights.name: Fatehpur Sikri and the Buland Darwaza
spotlights.spot_it: A ghost city of red sandstone palaces and courtyards on a ridge, entered through a giant arched gate at the top of a flight of steps.
spotlights.story_md: Akbar had no surviving son until the Sufi saint **Salim Chishti** of Sikri prayed for him; Prince Salim, later Jahangir, was born in **1569**. In gratitude Akbar built a new capital beside the saint's hermitage from **1571**. The **Buland Darwaza**, about **54 m** high from the ground, marks his conquest of Gujarat. Within about 15 years the court left. The usual explanation is a water shortage, but historians also point to Akbar's wars in the northwest. The saint's white marble tomb still stands in the mosque courtyard, and visitors tie threads to its stone screens to ask for children.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a perfectly preserved Mughal city, frozen in the 1580s.
spotlights.memory_hook: A capital built for a baby, abandoned in fifteen years.

sections.title: The nawabs of Lucknow
sections.intro_md:
As Mughal power faded in the 18th century, its governors became kings in all but name. In **Awadh**, the province around Lucknow and Faizabad, a line of Shia nawabs ruled from **1722** until the British annexed the state in **1856**. They had money from the richest farmland in India, and they spent it on buildings, poets, musicians, cooks and courtesans.

Lucknow became the place where Urdu poetry, the Kathak dance, the thumri song and slow-cooked *dum* food were polished into the forms we know. It also became a byword for refinement carried to the point of comedy: the Lucknow joke is two gentlemen saying *pehle aap*, 'after you', until the train leaves without them.

The British kept squeezing the nawabs for money and territory, then removed the last one in 1856 on grounds of misrule. The anger this caused fed directly into the rebellion of 1857.

spotlights.name: Bara Imambara and its maze
spotlights.spot_it: A vast, plain-faced hall behind a triple gateway, with a mosque beside it and a stepwell below.
spotlights.story_md: In **1784** famine hit Awadh. Nawab **Asaf-ud-Daula** answered with a public works project: a huge *imambara*, a hall for Shia mourning during Muharram. Its central hall is about **50 m** long and **15 m** high, one of the largest vaulted rooms in the world built without beams or iron. To carry the load, the builders put a maze in the roof: the **Bhool Bhulaiya**, a warren of narrow passages and identical doorways. Local lore says some workers tore down at night what others built by day, to stretch the wages; there is no record of it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is famine relief turned into architecture, and still a working religious building.
spotlights.memory_hook: A maze on the roof holds up a hall with no beams.

spotlights.name: Wajid Ali Shah
spotlights.spot_it: Painted portraits of a heavy-set king in jewels and silk, often with a pearl-strung turban.
spotlights.story_md: The last king of Awadh was a poet, a composer and a dancer. He wrote dozens of books, staged musical dramas called *rahas* in which he performed himself, and patronised the Kathak masters whose family line runs to Birju Maharaj. The British deposed him in **1856**, calling his government corrupt. He was exiled to **Metiabruz** in Kolkata, where he rebuilt a small Lucknow and lived for 30 years. Kolkata biryani's potato is credited to his cooks, without firm evidence. The farewell song *Babul mora* is attributed to him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His fall triggered the anger of 1857, and his court shaped north Indian music and dance.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dancing king, exiled to Kolkata, took his kitchen with him.

sections.title: 1857 and the long road to freedom
sections.intro_md:
The great rebellion of **1857** began in UP and was fought hardest here. On **10 May** soldiers at **Meerut** shot their officers and marched to Delhi. Within weeks Awadh, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly and Allahabad had risen. In **Kanpur**, the rebel leader Nana Sahib's forces killed British men at the river ghat and later women and children at the **Bibighar**; British reprisals then killed thousands of Indians, many without trial. In **Lucknow**, **Begum Hazrat Mahal** led the resistance in the name of her young son.

UP stayed at the centre of the national movement. Allahabad's **Anand Bhavan** was the Nehru family home and a Congress headquarters. The violence at **Chauri Chaura** in 1922 made Gandhi halt his first mass campaign. Revolutionaries of the **Kakori** train action of 1925, Ram Prasad Bismil and Ashfaqulla Khan, a Hindu and a Muslim, were hanged in 1927 and are remembered together.

spotlights.name: The Residency, Lucknow
spotlights.spot_it: Roofless brick ruins in a quiet park, walls still pocked by cannon shot.
spotlights.story_md: When Awadh rose in **1857**, about 3,000 British and loyal Indian soldiers and civilians took refuge in the British Resident's compound. They were besieged for nearly **five months**. Disease, snipers and mines dug under the walls killed hundreds; the commander Henry Lawrence died in the first week. A relief force fought in late September but was itself trapped. Only in **November** was the garrison evacuated. The British left the ruins as they were, as a memorial. After independence, a plaque to the Indian fighters was added.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most complete battlefield of 1857 and a site read very differently by Britain and India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five months under siege, and the ruins were left on purpose.

spotlights.name: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi
spotlights.spot_it: A woman on horseback with a sword, and in some versions a child tied to her back: the image on countless statues.
spotlights.story_md: When the Raja of Jhansi died in **1853**, the British refused to recognise his adopted son and annexed the state. His widow, **Lakshmibai**, protested for years and then, in **1858**, led its defence. When Jhansi fell she escaped with her son, joined the rebel commander Tatya Tope and helped take Gwalior. She died fighting near Gwalior on **18 June 1858**. A British officer who fought her called her the most dangerous of the rebel leaders. The leap on horseback from the fort walls is legend; the courage is not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She became India's symbol of resistance, and a model for women in uniform.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sword in hand, son on her back: the queen the Empire feared most.

spotlights.name: Chauri Chaura, 4 February 1922
spotlights.spot_it: A memorial pillar and park in a small town near Gorakhpur.
spotlights.story_md: During Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement, police fired on protesters at the market town of **Chauri Chaura**. The crowd fought back, trapped the policemen in their station and set it on fire. **22 policemen** died. Gandhi, horrified, called off the entire nationwide movement days later, against the wishes of most Congress leaders. The British tried more than 200 people; 19 were finally hanged. For decades Indian textbooks treated the event as a riot. Since **2021** the state has marked it as part of the freedom struggle, with a centenary memorial.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One night in a small town stopped a national movement.
spotlights.memory_hook: A burning police station made Gandhi hit the brakes.

sections.title: The state that makes prime ministers
sections.intro_md:
The British stitched this territory together as the **North-Western Provinces** and then the **United Provinces of Agra and Oudh** (1902). On **24 January 1950** it became Uttar Pradesh. In **2000** its Himalayan districts left to form Uttarakhand.

With 80 Lok Sabha seats, UP decides national elections. **Nine** of India's prime ministers have sat for UP constituencies, from Jawaharlal Nehru (Phulpur) and Indira Gandhi (Rae Bareli) to Atal Bihari Vajpayee (Lucknow) and Narendra Modi (Varanasi).

Congress ruled almost without break until **1989**. Then caste politics (**Mulayam Singh Yadav**'s Samajwadi Party, **Kanshi Ram** and **Mayawati**'s BSP) and the Ram temple movement, which built the BJP, broke it. Since **2017** the BJP's **Yogi Adityanath** has governed with large majorities. Yet in the **2024** national election the Samajwadi Party won more UP seats than the BJP, including **Faizabad**, the constituency that contains Ayodhya.

spotlights.name: Mayawati
spotlights.when: Born 1956; chief minister four times between 1995 and 2012
spotlights.spot_it: A woman with short cropped hair in a pale salwar kameez, a handbag on her arm, often beside a giant stone elephant.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Delhi to a Dalit family, Mayawati was a schoolteacher studying for the civil services when **Kanshi Ram** recruited her into politics. In **1995** she became the first Dalit woman to be chief minister of any Indian state. In **2007** her BSP won a majority on its own by courting Brahmins as well as Dalits. She built enormous memorial parks in Lucknow and Noida, filled with statues of Dalit icons, stone elephants (the party symbol) and statues of herself. Critics saw vanity; supporters saw Dalit pride in stone. The BSP won no Lok Sabha seats in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She proved a Dalit woman could run India's largest state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A schoolteacher who put stone elephants all over Lucknow.

spotlights.name: Yogi Adityanath
spotlights.spot_it: A shaven-headed monk in saffron robes, at a podium or on a dais.
spotlights.story_md: Born **Ajay Mohan Bisht** in what is now Uttarakhand, he became a disciple at the **Gorakhnath Math** in Gorakhpur and, in **2014**, its head priest. He was elected to Parliament from Gorakhpur five times from **1998**. The BJP made him chief minister after its landslide in **2017**. In **2022** he became the first UP chief minister in decades to win re-election after a full term, and he is now the state's longest continuously serving chief minister. His government is known for expressways, investment summits, renaming cities and a hard line on crime, criticised by rights groups over police encounter killings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He combines the roles of temple head and head of government.
spotlights.memory_hook: The abbot of Gorakhpur runs a state of 240 million.

sections.title: The cradle of Hindi and Urdu
sections.intro_md:
Standard **Hindi** and **Urdu** both grew out of **Khari Boli**, the speech of the country around Delhi and Meerut. Written in Devanagari with a Sanskrit vocabulary it is Hindi; in Persian script with Persian and Arabic words it is Urdu; spoken on the street, the two are nearly the same language. Hindi is UP's official language, and **Urdu** has been the second official language since **1989**. In 2011 about **94%** of people gave Hindi as their mother tongue and about **5%** Urdu.

Under 'Hindi' sit older literary languages that are still spoken at home. **Awadhi**, around Lucknow and Ayodhya, carried Tulsidas's Ramayana. **Braj Bhasha**, around Mathura, was the language of Krishna poetry for 400 years. **Bhojpuri**, in the east, travelled with indentured labourers to Mauritius, Fiji and the Caribbean and now drives a film and music industry. **Bundeli** is spoken in the south.

spotlights.name: Tulsidas and the Ramcharitmanas
spotlights.spot_it: Handwritten Devanagari verses in four-line chaupai stanzas, often recited in a sing-song by a reader at a shrine.
spotlights.story_md: In **1574**, on Ram's birthday in Ayodhya, the poet **Tulsidas** began retelling the Ramayana, not in Sanskrit but in **Awadhi**, the everyday speech of the region. Brahmins of Varanasi reportedly objected that sacred stories belonged in Sanskrit. The people disagreed. The *Ramcharitmanas*, 'the lake of Ram's deeds', became the most read book in north India; the Ramlila plays act it out, and families recite it whole in a few days. Tulsidas lived at **Tulsi Ghat** in Varanasi, where his house and slippers are still shown to visitors.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how most Hindi speakers know the story of Ram.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Ramayana in the language of the street, and the street never let it go.

spotlights.name: Kabir
spotlights.spot_it: A weaver at his loom, in old miniatures, often with a disciple; and two-line verses, dohas, quoted in every school.
spotlights.story_md: Kabir was a **weaver** in Varanasi, raised in a Muslim family, who mocked both priests and mullahs. His short couplets are still the most quoted lines in Hindi. Varanasi held that dying there meant liberation, and that dying in **Maghar** meant rebirth as a donkey. So Kabir went to Maghar to die. Legend says Hindu and Muslim followers fought over his body, lifted the sheet and found only flowers, which they divided. Maghar today has a Hindu samadhi and a Muslim tomb standing side by side.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the voice of a faith beyond religion, read by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs alike.
spotlights.memory_hook: He chose the town of donkeys to die in, and left only flowers.

spotlights.name: Premchand
spotlights.spot_it: A thin man with a large moustache in a plain kurta and cap, in an old studio photograph.
spotlights.story_md: Born **Dhanpat Rai** in the village of Lamhi near Varanasi in **1880**, he first wrote in Urdu as 'Nawab Rai'. In **1907** the British confiscated his story collection *Soz-e-Watan* as seditious and had copies burned, so he took a new name: **Premchand**. He wrote about 300 short stories and novels about farmers, debt, caste and widows, in plain Hindustani. His last novel, *Godaan* (1936), about a peasant who dreams of owning a cow, is still the most taught novel in Hindi. *Kafan*, 'The Shroud', is one of the bleakest short stories in any Indian language.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He brought ordinary village life into Hindi and Urdu fiction.
spotlights.memory_hook: The British burned his book, so he changed his name.

sections.title: Holy cities, and the fights over them
sections.intro_md:
Uttar Pradesh holds more of Hinduism's sacred geography than any other state. **Varanasi** is Shiva's city, where dying is believed to bring liberation. **Ayodhya** is Ram's birthplace by tradition. **Mathura** and **Vrindavan** are Krishna's childhood country. **Prayagraj** has the Sangam. Sarnath and Kushinagar are among Buddhism's holiest places.

UP also has the largest Muslim population of any state, about **38 million** in 2011, **19.3%** of its people. It produced two of South Asia's most influential Islamic schools, **Deoband** and the **Barelvi** movement of Bareilly, as well as the modernist **Aligarh Muslim University**. Lucknow is a centre of Shia Islam in India.

The Babri Masjid in Ayodhya was demolished in **1992**; the Supreme Court gave the site for a temple in **2019**. Disputes over the mosques next to the Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi and the Krishna Janmabhoomi in Mathura are still in the courts.

spotlights.name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A small temple with gold-plated spires in a dense old quarter, now opening onto a wide new stone plaza that runs down to the river.
spotlights.story_md: The temple of Shiva as 'lord of the universe' has been destroyed and rebuilt several times. The **Gyanvapi Mosque** next door was built on Aurangzeb's orders in **1669** on the ruins of an earlier temple, whose wall is still visible in the mosque's back. The present temple was built in **1780** by **Ahilyabai Holkar**, queen of Indore. In **1835** Maharaja **Ranjit Singh** gave about a tonne of gold to plate its spires. In **December 2021** a government corridor cleared about 300 buildings to connect the temple to the ghats. Courts are still hearing cases over the mosque.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the holiest Shiva temple for many Hindus and a flashpoint of history.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen from Indore built it, a Sikh king gilded it.

spotlights.name: Ram Mandir, Ayodhya
spotlights.when: Consecrated 22 January 2024; spire flag raised 25 November 2025
spotlights.spot_it: A three-storey temple of pale pink sandstone with a tall curved spire and rows of carved pillars.
spotlights.story_md: The site was claimed by Hindus as Ram's birthplace and held the **Babri Masjid**, a mosque built in **1528**. A crowd tore the mosque down on **6 December 1992**, setting off riots that killed about 2,000 people across India. In **November 2019** the Supreme Court gave the land to a trust for a temple and five acres elsewhere for a mosque. The temple, in the north Indian **Nagara** style, uses pink sandstone from Rajasthan and, its builders say, no steel. The idol of the child Ram, carved in black stone by **Arun Yogiraj** of Mysuru, was consecrated on **22 January 2024**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most politically charged building in modern India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five centuries of argument, settled in pink stone.

spotlights.name: Vrindavan and the Banke Bihari temple
spotlights.when: Temple 1864; Krishna cult since the 16th century
spotlights.spot_it: Packed lanes, monkeys snatching glasses, and a temple where a curtain is drawn across the deity every few minutes.
spotlights.story_md: Vrindavan is the forest where Krishna grew up as a cowherd, and the town has more than **5,000 temples** by local count. In the **Banke Bihari** temple the curtain in front of the image is pulled shut every few minutes. The explanation devotees give: if you gaze too long, Krishna may follow you home. Vrindavan is also known for thousands of **widows**, many from Bengal, who came or were sent here to live out their lives in prayer; since 2013 they have been invited to play Holi, which widows traditionally could not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the heart of Krishna devotion, and a mirror of how India treats widows.
spotlights.memory_hook: A god behind a curtain, so he will not follow you home.

sections.title: Kathak, thumri and the theatre of Ram
sections.intro_md:
North Indian classical music and dance took much of their present shape in the courts and temple towns of UP. **Kathak**, from the *kathakars* or storytellers, grew in temple courtyards and then in the courts of Lucknow and Jaipur. **Thumri**, the light-classical love song, was refined in Lucknow and Varanasi. The **Benaras gharana** gave the tabla some of its greatest players, and Varanasi produced the sitarist **Ravi Shankar** and the singers **Girija Devi** and **Chhannulal Mishra**.

Theatre lives outdoors. Every autumn thousands of **Ramlilas** act out the Ramayana on village grounds, and in **Braj** the *Raslila* acts out Krishna's childhood. UNESCO inscribed Ramlila as intangible heritage in **2008**. The folk stage of **Nautanki**, sung in loud verse to the beat of the nagara drum, once toured every fair in the state.

spotlights.name: Kathak, Lucknow style
spotlights.spot_it: A dancer spinning on the spot with straight legs, skirt flaring, then stopping dead on the beat; ankle bells chattering through fast footwork.
spotlights.story_md: Kathak is the only Indian classical dance in which dancers spin dozens of times in a row without losing the beat, and the only one danced in a north Indian court costume, the *angarkha* and churidar. Its footwork, *tatkar*, is a conversation with the tabla; dancers may wear more than **100 bells** on each ankle. The **Lucknow gharana**, shaped in the court of **Wajid Ali Shah**, stresses delicate expression and grace; the Jaipur style stresses speed and power. Watch for the *thaat*, the opening pose, and the *tihai*, a phrase repeated three times to land exactly on the first beat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is UP's classical dance and the one Hindi cinema borrows most.
spotlights.memory_hook: Spin, stamp, freeze: Kathak lands on the beat like a cat.

spotlights.name: Pandit Birju Maharaj
spotlights.spot_it: A round-faced man with long hair, in a kurta, his face moving through emotions while his hands barely move.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **1938** into the family of the Lucknow court dancers Kalka Prasad and Bindadin, Birju Maharaj lost his father at nine and was teaching dance by his early teens. He became the face of Kathak for 60 years. He choreographed the dance scenes in Satyajit Ray's *Shatranj Ke Khilari* (1977), set in the last days of Wajid Ali Shah's court, and later *Devdas* (2002). He also played drums, sang, wrote poetry and painted. He received the **Padma Vibhushan** in **1986** and died in **January 2022**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He carried the Lucknow court style into the modern concert hall and film.
spotlights.memory_hook: The court dancer's grandson who choreographed Satyajit Ray.

spotlights.name: Ramlila of Ramnagar
spotlights.spot_it: Masked and crowned boy actors on a field at dusk, lit by oil lamps, with a crowd walking behind them to the next scene.
spotlights.story_md: Across the river from Varanasi, the Maharaja of Benares has staged the Ramayana every year since the **1830s**. It lasts about **31 days**. The whole town is the stage: different places stand for Ayodhya, the forest, Lanka, and the audience walks from one to the next. There are no microphones and no electric lights. The lead roles are played by young Brahmin boys, and for the month they are treated as gods; people touch their feet. The Maharaja attends in state, and a performance does not begin until he arrives.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most complete and traditional Ramlila, and a model for UNESCO's listing.
spotlights.memory_hook: A month-long play where the audience walks to Lanka.

spotlights.name: Ustad Bismillah Khan
spotlights.spot_it: An old man in a cap and kurta, cheeks puffed, playing a short wooden reed pipe with a flared bell.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **Dumraon**, Bihar, in **1916**, Bismillah Khan came to Varanasi as a child to learn from his uncle, who played the **shehnai** at the Kashi Vishwanath temple. He took a reed pipe used at weddings and made it a concert instrument. On the night of **15 August 1947** he played at the Red Fort as India became independent. A devout Muslim, he played at Hindu temples all his life and practised on the ghats of the Ganga. Offered a life in America, he is said to have asked if they could bring the Ganga too. He received the **Bharat Ratna** in **2001** and was buried with a shehnai.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the sound of Indian auspicious occasions, and of Varanasi's shared culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: He would leave Varanasi only if the Ganga came too.

sections.title: Silk, thread, brass and glass
sections.intro_md:
Uttar Pradesh has more **Geographical Indication** tags than any other state: **77** by April 2025, according to state figures, and the Varanasi region alone holds about **32**. In **2018** the state launched **One District One Product**, giving each of its 75 districts a signature craft or food to promote, from Moradabad brass to Kannauj perfume.

Most of these crafts are clusters, whole towns organised around one product, with skills passed down within families and often within one community: Muslim Ansari weavers in Varanasi, women embroiderers in the lanes of Lucknow, glass workers in Firozabad. Wages are low, child labour has been documented in several clusters, and machine copies undercut handwork.

spotlights.name: Banarasi silk sari
spotlights.when: Brocade weaving flourished from the Mughal period; GI 2009
spotlights.spot_it: Heavy silk with gold and silver *zari* motifs of flowers and leaves, a wide decorated border and a dense end panel.
spotlights.story_md: A traditional Banarasi is woven on a pit or frame handloom with a punched-card **jacquard** above it, and can take **15 days to six months** to finish depending on the design. The richest kind, *kadhua*, weaves each motif separately by hand, so the back is clean. Many weavers are from the Muslim **Ansari** community; many wearers are Hindu brides. Powerloom copies from Surat and China, sold as Banarasi, have hurt the handloom families badly. 'Banaras Brocades and Sarees' received a **GI tag in 2009**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's classic wedding sari, and its making is a shared Hindu-Muslim craft.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bride in Delhi, a weaver in Varanasi, six months of one sari.

spotlights.name: Chikankari of Lucknow
spotlights.spot_it: Fine white thread embroidery on pale muslin or cotton, with shadow work that makes flowers glow through the cloth.
spotlights.story_md: Chikankari begins with a wooden block: the pattern is stamped onto cloth in a washable blue dye. Women then embroider it, often at home, using more than **30 stitches**. The most famous is *bakhiya*, shadow work done from the back so the motif appears as a soft shadow on the front. Knot stitches called *phanda* and *murri* sit like tiny seeds; *jali* makes a net by pulling threads apart without cutting. Legend credits **Nur Jahan** with bringing it from Persia; there is no evidence. The work is washed at the end, the blue disappears and only white remains. Its **GI tag** came in **2008**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Lucknow's signature, worn from offices to weddings.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stamped in blue, stitched in white, washed until the blue is gone.

spotlights.name: Moradabad brass
spotlights.when: Export boom from the late 19th century
spotlights.spot_it: Engraved and enamelled brass vases, plates and lamps, gleaming gold, piled in workshop stacks.
spotlights.story_md: Moradabad is called *Peetal Nagri*, the brass city. Its workshops cast, beat, engrave and enamel brass and other metals, and the city exports home decor and tableware to the United States, Europe and the Gulf. A large share of the workforce is Muslim artisans working in small home units. The craft has moved with markets, from Victorian trays to modern aluminium and iron home goods, but still keeps hand engraving (*nakkashi*). Brass from Moradabad is one of the ODOP signature products.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of India's biggest handicraft export hubs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Peetal Nagri: a whole city that shines.

spotlights.name: Bhadohi carpets
spotlights.when: Hand-knotted carpet belt since the 16th to 19th centuries; GI 2010
spotlights.spot_it: A weaver at a vertical loom tying wool knots row by row, with a paper pattern pinned above.
spotlights.story_md: The belt around **Bhadohi**, Mirzapur and Varanasi is India's largest centre of hand-knotted and hand-tufted carpets, and is known as the carpet city. Legend says Persian weavers stopping on the Grand Trunk Road taught the craft in Mughal times; it boomed under British exporters in the 19th century. A good hand-knotted carpet can have hundreds of knots per square inch and take months. 'Bhadohi hand-made carpet' received a **GI tag** in **2010**. The trade was hit hard when its exposure to child labour became an international campaign in the 1990s, which led to the Rugmark (now GoodWeave) label.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a major export, and a case study in how buyers can change labour practice.
spotlights.memory_hook: Months of knots, and a label that asks who tied them.

spotlights.name: Kannauj attar and the smell of rain
spotlights.spot_it: Copper stills sealed with clay over wood fires, bamboo pipes running to receiving pots cooled in water.
spotlights.story_md: Kannauj makes **attar**, natural perfume distilled into sandalwood oil, using the *deg-bhapka* method: copper stills (*deg*) sealed with clay, steam passing through bamboo pipes into a receiving flask (*bhapka*) sitting in water. Roses, jasmine, vetiver and kewda all go in. Its strangest product is **mitti attar**: baked clay discs from local ponds are distilled to capture the smell of first rain on dry earth, the scent known as *petrichor*. A distiller sits up all night watching the fires by feel. Kannauj attar received a **GI tag** in **2014**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the last places that makes perfume this way.
spotlights.memory_hook: A town that can bottle the smell of rain.

sections.title: Kebabs, chaat and a sweet made of dew
sections.intro_md:
UP eats in two broad registers. The **Awadhi** kitchen of Lucknow is the cooking of the nawabs: meat slow-cooked in sealed pots (*dum*), kebabs so soft they need no chewing, breads like sheermal enriched with milk and saffron. The everyday food of the state is vegetarian and fried: puri and potato curry, kachori, chaat, and a sweet shop on every corner.

Each city has its own claims. Lucknow has kebabs and biryani; Varanasi has kachori-sabzi for breakfast, *malaiyo* in winter and paan after every meal; Agra has petha; Mathura has peda made of reduced milk. In the east, *litti chokha*, wheat balls stuffed with roasted gram flour and eaten with mashed aubergine, is shared with Bihar. Mango season is a festival of its own: the **Dasheri** mango from **Malihabad** near Lucknow got a GI tag in 2009.

Kachori-sabzi and jalebi, malaiyo, paan, lassi in a clay cup
Petha, bedmi puri with potato curry

spotlights.name: Galouti kebab
spotlights.when: Lucknow court cuisine; Tunday's shop from 1905
spotlights.spot_it: Small, dark, very soft minced-meat patties, crisp at the edges, served on a thin flaky paratha.
spotlights.story_md: *Galouti* means 'melts in the mouth'. Minced meat is tenderised with raw papaya, blended with a long list of spices and shallow-fried on a griddle. The famous story says it was invented for a toothless nawab who still wanted kebabs; it is a legend, attached to more than one nawab. The best-known maker is **Tunday Kababi** in the old city, opened in **1905** by **Haji Murad Ali**, who had one arm (*tunda*). The family says its spice mix is a secret held by women of the household and contains over 100 ingredients.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the signature of Awadhi cooking.
spotlights.memory_hook: A kebab for a nawab with no teeth.

spotlights.name: Agra petha
spotlights.when: Agra speciality for over a century
spotlights.spot_it: Translucent white cubes of candied ash gourd, sometimes flavoured with saffron or rose, sold in boxes near the Taj.
spotlights.story_md: Petha is made from **ash gourd** (white pumpkin), pricked, soaked in lime water to firm it, and then boiled in sugar syrup until it turns glassy. It is crisp outside and soft inside. Agra has hundreds of petha shops, and the name **Panchhi** is so famous that dozens of shops copy it. A popular legend says Shah Jahan's cooks made it for the workers building the Taj; there is no historical record. It is a vegan sweet that keeps for weeks, which is why it became the classic gift to take home from Agra.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is what every visitor to the Taj carries home.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pumpkin turned to glass, in a box from Agra.

spotlights.name: Banarasi paan
spotlights.spot_it: A betel leaf folded into a neat triangle around lime, catechu, areca nut and sweet fillings, handed over by a seller at a tiny stall.
spotlights.story_md: In Varanasi, paan is an after-meal ritual and a conversation. The leaf is aged and cured, so it turns soft and pale. The seller paints on slaked lime and catechu, adds fennel, cardamom and other fillings, folds it into a cone or triangle and hands it straight into your mouth. Locals chew slowly and spit red; the stains on walls are part of the city's palette. The 1978 film song *Khaike paan Banaraswala* made it national. **Banarasi paan** received a **GI tag** in **2023**. Areca nut is a carcinogen, so the tobacco-free sweet paan is the one to try.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a social ritual and Varanasi's most famous taste.
spotlights.memory_hook: Folded, painted, popped in the mouth: Banaras in a leaf.

spotlights.name: Malaiyo, the winter dew sweet
spotlights.when: Winter mornings only, roughly November to February
spotlights.spot_it: A cloud-like saffron foam served in a small clay cup, topped with pistachio, gone from stalls by late morning.
spotlights.story_md: Malaiyo can be made only on cold winter nights. Milk is boiled, cooled and left out under the open sky, where tradition says the **dew** helps it set. Before dawn it is churned by hand into a light foam with sugar and saffron and sold in clay cups called *kulhad*. It melts almost as soon as it touches the tongue, and vendors sell out by mid-morning. Lucknow calls the same idea *makhan malai*, and Delhi *daulat ki chaat*. Whether the dew really matters is debated; the cold certainly does.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a seasonal ritual that cannot be industrialised.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sweet made of milk, sky and a cold night.

sections.title: Festivals of light, colour and sticks
sections.intro_md:
UP's festival calendar is the Hindu calendar at its most intense, with Muslim, Buddhist and Sikh observances woven through it. Holi starts a week early in Braj. Diwali brings the world record lamp count in Ayodhya and, a fortnight later, the ghats of Varanasi light up for the gods. In the east, Chhath brings women to riverbanks at sunrise. In Lucknow, the Shia mourning month of **Muharram** fills the old city with processions, *tazias* and elegies. In the monsoon month of Shravan, millions of *kanwariyas* walk through western UP carrying Ganga water to Shiva temples.

Many festivals are now state-branded record attempts, a modern twist on kings competing to stage the grandest show.

data.name: Magh Mela and Kumbh bathing days at Prayagraj
Lathmar Holi in Barsana and Nandgaon, then Holi
Dev Deepawali in Varanasi, Chhath in the east

spotlights.name: Lathmar Holi of Barsana
spotlights.when: About a week before Holi, February or March
spotlights.spot_it: Women in bright saris swinging long bamboo sticks at men crouched under round leather shields, all drenched in pink and yellow colour.
spotlights.story_md: Barsana is Radha's village and Nandgaon is Krishna's, 8 km apart. In the story, Krishna and his friends came to tease Radha's friends and were chased off with sticks. Every spring the men of **Nandgaon** come to Barsana, sing provocative songs, and the women of Barsana beat them with *lathis*. The men defend themselves with shields and are not allowed to fight back. The next day the roles reverse in Nandgaon. The blows are real but ritual, and the crowd of visitors is now in the hundreds of thousands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a role reversal festival, women chasing men, staged for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Barsana, Holi is when the women carry sticks.

spotlights.name: Dev Deepawali, Varanasi
spotlights.spot_it: Kilometres of river steps outlined in tiny oil lamps, reflected in the dark Ganga, with boats crowded with watchers.
spotlights.story_md: On the full moon of Kartik, a fortnight after Diwali, Varanasi celebrates the 'Diwali of the gods', when the gods are said to come down to bathe in the Ganga. Every ghat is lined with clay lamps, more than a million in recent years, and lit at dusk. Boats jam the river to watch. A grand Ganga aarti is performed at Dashashwamedh. The festival was a local affair until the 1980s and 1990s; it is now one of the biggest tourist events in the state, and boat fares on the night run to many times the usual price.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns Varanasi's whole river front into a single picture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Diwali for the gods, two weeks after ours.

spotlights.name: Deepotsav, Ayodhya
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of glowing clay lamps covering every step of a river front, filmed from drones, with a laser show above.
spotlights.story_md: In **2017** the state began lighting lamps on the ghats of the Sarayu river in Ayodhya on Diwali eve: **171,000** that year. The count has risen every year. On **19 October 2025**, Guinness officials using drones verified **2,617,215** lamps across 56 ghats, a world record, along with a second record for 2,128 people performing aarti together. More than **33,000** volunteers, many of them university students, place, fill and light the lamps. Critics ask about the cost and the oil; supporters see Ayodhya being turned into a pilgrim city on a national scale.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how festivals have become instruments of state branding.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two and a half million lamps, counted by drone.

spotlights.name: Evening Ganga aarti at Dashashwamedh
spotlights.when: Every evening, in its present form since about 1991
spotlights.spot_it: A row of young priests in saffron and gold on wooden platforms, swinging tall brass lamps in unison, conch shells, bells and smoke.
spotlights.story_md: Every evening at sunset, seven priests stand on platforms at **Dashashwamedh Ghat** and perform the aarti to the river: incense, then multi-tiered brass lamps swung in great arcs, then yak-tail whisks and peacock fans, to bells, conch shells and chanting. The choreographed version dates only from about **1991**, when a local trust organised it; before that the aarti was a simpler temple rite. It has since been copied in Haridwar, Rishikesh, Prayagraj and even on the Sabarmati. Thousands watch from the steps and from boats every night.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most watched daily ritual in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven priests, seven lamps, one river, every single night.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
UP is young, rural and on the move. In 2011 about **78%** of people lived in villages. Families are large by Indian standards: women in UP have about **2.4** children on average (NFHS-5, 2019-21), down from 2.7 five years earlier and close to replacement level in the cities, but still among the highest of any state. About **40%** of children under five are stunted.

UP is also India's biggest exporter of people. The 2011 census counted more migrants leaving UP for other states than from anywhere else, to the building sites, factories and taxi stands of Delhi, Mumbai, Punjab and Gujarat. When the 2020 lockdown shut those cities, more than three million came home.

Caste still organises marriage, politics and much of village life. Dalits are about **21%** of the population (2011); backward castes are generally estimated at around 40%, though no census has counted them since 1931.

spotlights.name: Lucknowi tehzeeb: 'pehle aap'
spotlights.when: Court culture of the 18th and 19th centuries
spotlights.spot_it: A slight bow with a cupped hand raised to the forehead (*adab*), soft-spoken Urdu with elaborate polite forms, and a lot of 'you first'.
spotlights.story_md: *Tehzeeb* means refinement, and Lucknow's version is a code of manners inherited from the Awadh court: the *adab* greeting, the formal *aap* rather than *tum*, invitations repeated several times before they count, and poetry quoted in ordinary speech. The famous joke is about two Lucknow gentlemen at a station, each insisting *pehle aap*, 'after you', until the train leaves without them. No survey measures politeness, so treat the stereotype with care: modern Lucknow traffic is as pushy as anywhere. But the forms are real, and many families still teach them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living memory of court culture, worn as civic pride.
spotlights.memory_hook: After you, no, after you: and the train has gone.

spotlights.name: Manikarnika Ghat and dying in Kashi
spotlights.spot_it: Smoke rising from several open pyres on a riverside platform, stacks of firewood above, bodies on bamboo stretchers wrapped in orange and white.
spotlights.story_md: Hindus believe that anyone who dies in Varanasi is freed from the cycle of rebirth. **Manikarnika** is the city's main cremation ghat, and its fires are said by locals never to go out. The cremations are managed by the **Dom** community, whose leaders were once wealthy and still hold the sacred fire. There are guesthouses where the old and sick come to wait for death: the best known, **Kashi Labh Mukti Bhawan**, takes guests for about two weeks, and asks them to leave if they have not died by then. The 2016 film *Hotel Salvation* is set in one.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Varanasi treats death as a destination, not an ending.
spotlights.memory_hook: A guesthouse where you check in to die, with a two-week limit.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
UP has produced prime ministers, poets, film stars and athletes out of proportion even to its size. Allahabad alone gave India Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, the poet Harivansh Rai Bachchan and his son Amitabh, and the hockey player Dhyan Chand. Varanasi gave Ravi Shankar, Girija Devi and the tabla line of the Benaras gharana. Lucknow gave Birju Maharaj and a long line of Urdu poets; Gorakhpur gave **Firaq Gorakhpuri**, the first Urdu poet to win the Jnanpith Award (1969).

Cricket too: **Mohammed Shami** is from Amroha, **Kuldeep Yadav** from Kanpur, **Rinku Singh** from Aligarh.

spotlights.name: Jawaharlal Nehru and Anand Bhavan
spotlights.spot_it: A slim man in a long buttoned achkan with a rose in the buttonhole and a white Gandhi cap.
spotlights.story_md: Nehru was born in Allahabad in **1889** to **Motilal Nehru**, one of India's richest lawyers. The family home, **Anand Bhavan**, became a Congress headquarters in the freedom struggle; when Motilal gave the first house to the party, he built a second and gave it the same name. Nehru spent almost nine years in British prisons. As India's first prime minister, from **1947 to 1964**, he sat for **Phulpur**, near Allahabad. His daughter **Indira** was born at Anand Bhavan in **1917**; the house is now a museum.
spotlights.why_it_matters: UP's political dominance starts with this family and this house.
spotlights.memory_hook: One family, one Allahabad house, three prime ministers.

spotlights.name: Dhyan Chand

where.label: Born Allahabad; grew up in Jhansi

spotlights.spot_it: A lean hockey player in old flannel kit, crouched over the ball, stick held low.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Allahabad in **1905**, Dhyan Chand learned hockey in the army and practised at night by moonlight, the story goes, which gave him the nickname *Chand*, moon. He won Olympic gold in **1928**, **1932** and **1936**. His control was so close that officials in the Netherlands are said to have broken his stick to check for a magnet, a story told in several versions with no record behind it. The tale that Hitler offered him a German army post is also unverified. His birthday, **29 August**, is India's National Sports Day, and the top sports award has borne his name since **2021**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He was India's first global sporting star.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three Olympic golds, and they checked his stick for a magnet.

spotlights.name: Ravi Shankar
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling man cross-legged on a stage carpet with a long-necked sitar, a tabla player beside him.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Varanasi in **1920**, Ravi Shankar spent his teens dancing in his brother Uday Shankar's troupe in Paris, then gave it up to study sitar for years under **Allauddin Khan** at Maihar. He took Indian classical music to the West: he taught **George Harrison** of the Beatles, played at **Monterey** in **1967** and **Woodstock** in **1969**, and wrote the score for Satyajit Ray's Apu trilogy. He received the **Bharat Ratna** in **1999**. His daughters are the sitarist Anoushka Shankar and the singer Norah Jones.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made a Varanasi instrument part of world music.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Varanasi to Woodstock, carrying a sitar.

sections.title: Places to go beyond the obvious
sections.intro_md:
Everyone knows the Taj, Varanasi and Lucknow. The quieter UP is in the south, in **Bundelkhand**: a rocky plateau of forts, lakes built by the Chandela kings a thousand years ago, and towns where the ballads of the warrior brothers **Alha and Udal** are still sung in the monsoon. There is **Jhansi**'s fort, the Gupta temple at **Deogarh**, the hill fort of **Kalinjar** and the forest pilgrim town of **Chitrakoot**.

In the east there is the Buddhist circuit: Sarnath, **Sravasti**, Kushinagar and Kapilavastu near the Nepal border. In the west, **Mathura**, **Vrindavan**, **Govardhan** and **Barsana** make a Krishna circuit an hour from Agra. **Jaunpur** has the great 15th-century mosques of the Sharqi sultans. Best season: **October to March**. Summer is brutal, and winter mornings bring fog.

spotlights.name: Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh
spotlights.spot_it: A small, square, ruined stone shrine on a plinth, its walls carved with deep panels of Vishnu.
spotlights.story_md: Built around **500 CE** under the Guptas, this is one of the oldest surviving Hindu stone temples in north India and one of the first with a tower over the shrine, now mostly collapsed. Its three wall panels are masterpieces: **Vishnu asleep on the serpent Shesha**, Vishnu rescuing an elephant from a crocodile, and two sages in meditation. It stands near the Betwa river, close to a hill covered with Jain temples. Few tourists come, and you may have it to yourself.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where the north Indian temple began to take shape.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first temple tower in the north, and nobody queues.

spotlights.name: Kalinjar Fort
spotlights.when: Fortified from at least the Chandela period, 10th century
spotlights.spot_it: Long walls along a flat-topped hill, gateways and temple ruins inside, rock-cut sculptures above water tanks.
spotlights.story_md: Kalinjar sits on a flat-topped hill above the Bundelkhand plain and was one of the strongest forts in India. **Mahmud of Ghazni** besieged it in the 1020s. In **1545** the Afghan emperor **Sher Shah Suri**, who had driven the Mughal Humayun out of India, besieged it and was killed when a store of gunpowder exploded beside him. Akbar took it later. Inside are the Neelkanth temple, rock-cut images of Shiva, and spring-fed tanks that never dry.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It killed one of India's most capable emperors.
spotlights.memory_hook: The fort that blew up the man who beat the Mughals.

sections.title: How it earns
sections.intro_md:
UP is India's farm. It grows more **wheat**, **sugarcane** and **potatoes** and produces more **milk** than any other state. Most workers still depend on small, shrinking farms.

Industry is concentrated at the two ends. In the west, **Noida** and **Greater Noida**, on Delhi's edge, have become India's main hub for assembling mobile phones and electronics. **Kanpur**, once called the Manchester of the East for its textile mills, is now known for leather.

The state has bet heavily on roads: it now has the largest network of expressways in India, including the **Purvanchal** (2021) and the **Ganga Expressway**, opened in **April 2026**. Its first Economic Survey, in February 2026, set a goal of a **$1 trillion** economy. Per person, UP remains one of India's poorer states.

spotlights.name: Sugarcane belt of western UP
spotlights.when: Year-round; crushing season October to April
spotlights.spot_it: Walls of green cane taller than a person, bullock carts and tractor trolleys piled high, queues at a sugar mill gate.
spotlights.story_md: UP grows roughly **half of India's sugarcane** and in recent years has often been India's largest sugar producer, ahead of Maharashtra. Cane is the cash crop of the western districts, and its price, set by the state, is one of the most political numbers in UP. Mills often pay farmers late, and unpaid cane dues have swung elections. Leftover molasses goes into ethanol now blended with petrol across India. The jaggery, *gur*, of Muzaffarnagar has its own market, one of the largest in Asia.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Cane prices decide votes in the west of the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Taller than a man and sweeter than politics: western UP's cane.

spotlights.name: Noida, India's phone factory
spotlights.spot_it: Glass office towers and low factory sheds beside wide new roads, with metro lines on pillars overhead.
spotlights.story_md: **Noida**, the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority, was planned in **1976** as a satellite town for Delhi. In **July 2018** Narendra Modi and South Korea's president Moon Jae-in opened Samsung's expanded plant in Noida's Sector 81, which the company called the **world's largest mobile phone factory**. Dozens of other phone and component makers followed, and the state says more than half of India's mobile phones are now assembled in UP. Noida also houses film studios, IT parks, and the new international airport at nearby Jewar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a Delhi suburb into an electronics capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Delhi suburb that builds the phone in your pocket.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**January to February 2025:** the Maha Kumbh at Prayagraj, with a claimed **660 million** visits and the deadly crush of 29 January.

**19 October 2025:** a record **2.6 million** lamps at Ayodhya's Deepotsav. **2 October 2025:** the Banaras singer **Chhannulal Mishra** died at 89 in Mirzapur and was cremated at Manikarnika with state honours.

**25 November 2025:** Narendra Modi and RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat raised a saffron flag on the finished spire of the **Ram Mandir**, marking the end of construction.

**January 2026:** a special revision of the voter rolls dropped about **2.89 crore** names from the draft list, nearly one in five, for deaths, migration and duplicates; after claims, about **2.04 crore** stayed off the final roll. Opposition parties called it mass disenfranchisement.

**April and June 2026:** the **Ganga Expressway** and **Noida International Airport** opened. **October 2026:** the High Court gave the state three months to hold overdue **panchayat** elections. The assembly election is due in early **2027**.

spotlights.name: Ganga Expressway
spotlights.spot_it: A six-lane concrete highway running dead straight across flat farmland, with almost no traffic yet.
spotlights.story_md: The **594 km** Ganga Expressway, opened by the prime minister at Hardoi on **29 April 2026**, runs from **Meerut** in the west to **Prayagraj**, through **12 districts**. It cost about **₹36,230 crore** and is built for six lanes, expandable to eight. The state says it cuts the trip from about 10 to 12 hours to about **6**. It was meant to be ready for the 2025 Kumbh and missed that date. Like the **Purvanchal Expressway** (2021), where an Air Force transport plane landed on a built-in airstrip at its opening, it has an emergency runway stretch for fighter jets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the spine of UP's bet that roads will bring industry to the east.
spotlights.memory_hook: Meerut to Prayagraj in six hours, with a runway in the middle.

spotlights.name: Noida International Airport, Jewar
spotlights.spot_it: A long, low terminal with a sweeping roof, standing in open farmland south of Greater Noida.
spotlights.story_md: Delhi's second big airport is in UP. The **Noida International Airport** at Jewar, about 75 km from central Delhi, was inaugurated on **28 March 2026** and began commercial flights on **15 June 2026**, when IndiGo flew in from Lucknow. Phase one has one runway and a terminal for about **12 million** passengers a year; plans go to five runways, which would make it one of the largest airports in Asia. It was built by a Swiss operator, Zurich Airport. The opening slipped several times from 2024. International flights are expected to follow.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shifts part of Delhi's air traffic, and its jobs, into UP.
spotlights.memory_hook: Delhi's new airport has a UP postcode.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md: Legends stick to every monument in UP. The table tests six of them. Two deserve a line more. The **Black Taj**, a twin in black marble across the river, rests on one 17th-century traveller's remark; digs at **Mehtab Bagh** found a moonlight garden, not a foundation. The claim that the Taj was once a Shiva temple called **Tejo Mahalaya** comes from a 1960s writer and has been rejected by historians, the Archaeological Survey of India and the courts. And Hindi and Urdu are, in everyday speech, one language with two scripts.

sections.title: Recap: Uttar Pradesh in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. About **240 million** people and 80 Lok Sabha seats.
2. The **Kumbh** at Prayagraj: a claimed 660 million visits in 2025.
3. The Buddha taught at **Sarnath**; its **Lion Capital** is India's emblem.
4. Agra: **Taj Mahal**, Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri.
5. The **nawabs of Awadh** shaped kebabs, Kathak and thumri; their fall fed **1857**.
6. **Hindi and Urdu** grew from western UP's Khari Boli; Tulsidas wrote in Awadhi.
7. **Varanasi**, **Ayodhya** and **Vrindavan** anchor Hindu pilgrimage and its politics.
8. Banarasi silk, chikankari, Kannauj attar: the most **GI tags** of any state.
9. Nine prime ministers; since 2017, **Yogi Adityanath**; in 2024 the SP won most UP seats.
10. India's biggest farm state and phone factory, at half the national income per head.

quiz_bank.explanation: As famine relief, a public works project by Asaf-ud-Daula.

quiz_bank.prompt: Where did the rebellion of 1857 begin, on 10 May?
quiz_bank.explanation: Meerut, where sepoys shot their officers and marched to Delhi.

quiz_bank.prompt: What did Gandhi do after Chauri Chaura in 1922?
quiz_bank.explanation: He called off the Non-Cooperation Movement.

quiz_bank.prompt: How many prime ministers of India have sat for UP constituencies?
quiz_bank.explanation: Nine, from Nehru to Modi.

quiz_bank.prompt: UP seats in 2024: BJP won 33. Did the Samajwadi Party win more or fewer?
quiz_bank.explanation: The SP won 37.

quiz_bank.prompt: Spoken Hindi and spoken Urdu are largely the same language.
quiz_bank.explanation: Both grew from Khari Boli; they differ mainly in script and formal vocabulary.

quiz_bank.prompt: Why did Kabir go to Maghar to die?
quiz_bank.explanation: To mock the belief that dying there meant rebirth as a donkey.
options: To defy a superstition about it

quiz_bank.prompt: In which year was the Babri Masjid demolished?
quiz_bank.explanation: 6 December 1992.

quiz_bank.prompt: Who built the present Kashi Vishwanath temple, in 1780?
quiz_bank.explanation: Ahilyabai Holkar, queen of Indore.

quiz_bank.prompt: How long does the Ramlila of Ramnagar last?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 31 days, staged across the town.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which Kathak gharana grew in Wajid Ali Shah's court?
quiz_bank.explanation: The Lucknow gharana, known for grace and expression.

quiz_bank.prompt: Uttar Pradesh has more GI tags than any other state.
quiz_bank.explanation: About 77 by April 2025, by state figures.

quiz_bank.prompt: What does Kannauj's mitti attar smell of?
quiz_bank.explanation: Rain on dry earth; it is distilled from baked clay.

quiz_bank.prompt: What does 'galouti' mean?
quiz_bank.explanation: Melts in the mouth.

quiz_bank.prompt: When can you eat malaiyo in Varanasi?
quiz_bank.explanation: Only on winter mornings; it needs cold nights.

quiz_bank.prompt: About how many lamps were lit at Ayodhya's Deepotsav in October 2025?
quiz_bank.explanation: 2,617,215, a Guinness record.

quiz_bank.prompt: At Barsana's Lathmar Holi, men are allowed to hit back.
quiz_bank.explanation: Men only defend themselves with shields.

quiz_bank.prompt: Average number of children per woman in UP (NFHS-5)?
quiz_bank.explanation: 2.4, down from 2.7 in NFHS-4.

quiz_bank.prompt: The 2011 census found more people leaving UP for other states than any other state.
quiz_bank.explanation: UP is India's biggest source of interstate migrants.

quiz_bank.prompt: Dhyan Chand's birthday is celebrated as what?
quiz_bank.explanation: National Sports Day, 29 August.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which ruler was killed at Kalinjar in 1545?
quiz_bank.explanation: Sher Shah Suri, by an exploding store of gunpowder.

quiz_bank.prompt: Roughly what share of India's sugarcane does UP grow?
quiz_bank.explanation: Around half.

quiz_bank.prompt: What did Samsung open in Noida in 2018?
quiz_bank.explanation: What it called the world's largest mobile phone factory.

quiz_bank.prompt: About how many names were left off UP's draft voter roll in January 2026?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 2.89 crore, nearly one in five; about 2.04 crore stayed off the final roll.

quiz_bank.prompt: When did Noida International Airport start commercial flights?
