best_facts.fact: The UP government says about 660 million people bathed at the 2025 Maha Kumbh in 45 days. If even half that is right, it was the largest gathering in human history.
best_facts.why_surprising: More visits than the population of the EU and US combined.

best_facts.fact: India's national emblem, the four lions, is a 2,250-year-old sculpture dug out of the ground at Sarnath in 1905. Only three of the lions appear in the official drawing.
best_facts.why_surprising: The emblem on every passport is a buried UP artefact.

best_facts.fact: In the 2024 Lok Sabha election the BJP lost Faizabad, the seat that contains Ayodhya, five months after consecrating the Ram temple there.
best_facts.why_surprising: The temple town voted against the temple party.

best_facts.fact: The Taj Mahal's four minarets were built leaning very slightly outward, so that if they fell in an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb.
best_facts.why_surprising: A deliberate tilt hidden in plain sight.

best_facts.fact: Kabir chose to die in Maghar because people believed dying there made you a donkey in your next life. Maghar now has a Hindu samadhi and a Muslim tomb for him, side by side.
best_facts.why_surprising: A poet who used his death as a joke against superstition.

best_facts.fact: Kannauj distils baked clay to make mitti attar, a perfume that smells like first rain on dry earth.
best_facts.why_surprising: Someone bottled petrichor centuries before the word existed.

best_facts.fact: Sher Shah Suri, who had driven the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India, was killed in 1545 at the siege of Kalinjar when a store of gunpowder exploded beside him.
best_facts.why_surprising: The man who beat the Mughals was undone by his own explosives.

best_facts.fact: At Varanasi the Ganga bends to flow north, back toward the Himalaya, and the city stands on that sacred bend.
best_facts.why_surprising: A river that seems to turn round and look home.

best_facts.fact: Varanasi has guesthouses for people who come to die. The best known, Mukti Bhawan, gives guests about two weeks and asks them to leave if they are still alive.
best_facts.why_surprising: A hotel with a death deadline.

best_facts.fact: The Bara Imambara of Lucknow was a famine relief project of 1784. Its huge beamless hall is held up partly by a maze of passages built into its roof.
best_facts.why_surprising: A maze that is also a structural engineering trick.

best_facts.fact: Nine prime ministers of India have been elected from UP constituencies, from Nehru in Phulpur to Modi in Varanasi.
best_facts.why_surprising: One state has supplied most of India's prime ministers.

best_facts.fact: Dhanpat Rai became 'Premchand' because the British confiscated and burned his first story collection as seditious.
best_facts.why_surprising: A ban created a pen name.

best_facts.fact: In 2018 archaeologists at Sinauli near Meerut found 4,000-year-old burials with copper-sheathed coffins and wheeled vehicles; whether they are chariots is still argued.
best_facts.why_surprising: Possible chariots older than the Vedas, an hour from Delhi.

best_facts.fact: The sarus crane, UP's state bird, is the tallest flying bird in the world, standing up to about 1.8 m.
best_facts.why_surprising: Taller than most people, living in rice fields.

best_facts.fact: Bismillah Khan, a devout Muslim, played the shehnai at Hindu temples all his life, and played at the Red Fort on the night India became independent.
best_facts.why_surprising: The sound of Indian independence came from Varanasi.

best_facts.fact: Ayodhya's Deepotsav grew from 171,000 lamps in 2017 to 2,617,215 in 2025, a Guinness record counted by drone.
In the Banke Bihari temple at Vrindavan, a curtain is drawn across the deity every few minutes so that devotees do not stare too long.
best_facts.why_surprising: A god you are not allowed to look at for too long.

best_facts.fact: Malaiyo, a Varanasi milk foam, can only be made on cold winter nights and is sold out by mid-morning.
best_facts.why_surprising: A sweet that depends on the weather.

side_dish.title: How Awadhi crossed the ocean: Fiji Hindi
side_dish.body_md:
Between **1879 and 1916**, about 60,000 Indians were shipped to Fiji as indentured labourers, *girmitiyas*, a word made from the English 'agreement'. Most came from the districts of eastern UP and western Bihar: Basti, Gonda, Faizabad, Azamgarh, Ghazipur. They signed papers they could not read, spent months at sea, and worked five-year contracts on sugar plantations.

On the plantations, people who spoke Awadhi, Bhojpuri, Magahi and other dialects had to understand one another. What emerged was a new language, **Fiji Hindi**, built mainly on **Awadhi** with Bhojpuri mixed in, plus words from English and Fijian. Linguists call it a koine: a compromise variety formed when related dialects meet. It drops some of standard Hindi's grammar (gender agreement is simplified) and keeps old Awadhi forms that have faded in India.

The same thing happened, with different results, in **Mauritius**, **Trinidad**, **Guyana** and **Suriname**, where Bhojpuri dominated. In Suriname it became Sarnami. The songs went too: chutney music in Trinidad grew from Bhojpuri wedding songs.

Today about a third of Fiji's people are of Indian descent, and Fiji Hindi is taught in schools alongside English and iTaukei, the Fijian language. The Ramcharitmanas, carried in the bundles of the first labourers, is still recited in Fijian temples in the Awadhi of Tulsidas. A language from fields near Ayodhya now lives in the South Pacific.

offline_task.title: Make a quick Lucknow-style shami kebab at home
offline_task.body_md:
Galouti needs a skilled hand and a long list of spices. Its everyday cousin, the shami kebab, is easy and very Lucknow.

1. Boil 250 g minced mutton or chicken (or soaked black chana for a vegetarian version) with 3 tbsp chana dal, a small piece of ginger, 4 cloves of garlic, 2 dried red chillies, 1 bay leaf, 4 cloves, 1 small stick of cinnamon, 4 black peppercorns and salt, in just enough water, until the dal is soft and the pan is dry.
2. Cool, then grind to a smooth paste. Mix in a finely chopped small onion, coriander leaves, mint, a green chilli and half a teaspoon of garam masala. Add a beaten egg if the mixture is loose.
3. Shape into flat discs the size of your palm. Shallow-fry in ghee or oil on a hot tawa until deep brown on both sides.

Serve with thinly sliced onion, lemon and green chutney, wrapped in a paratha. Notice how soft it is: that softness is the Awadhi ideal, the reason a galouti 'melts'.
